The computational suite combines surface and bulk scattering modules to predict electromagnetic signatures in polymeric materials.
Geometric optics ray tracing is used for surface scattering when the size parameter α > 1.
Finite element methods solve Maxwell’s equations for scattering when α ≤ 1.
Surface roughness is statistically modeled using Gaussian distributions for peak and valley heights.
Atomic force microscope (AFM) scans can be used to input real surface profiles into simulations.
Increasing root mean squared (rms) surface roughness reduces mean hemispherical reflectance of PMMA surfaces.
Reflectance increases as the incident radiation angle approaches grazing incidence (85°).
Shadowing on rough surfaces increases non-linearly with incident angle and surface roughness.
The Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) is calculated from the differential reflection coefficient and geometric factors.
Direct computational methods predict material response to incident radiation; inverse methods design materials for desired responses.
The suite can simulate scattering from nanoscale fillers, pigments, fibers, and air voids within polymer matrices.
The geometric optics approximation requires about 1% of the CPU memory and 20% of the time compared to exact electromagnetic scattering solutions.
Multiple scattering and shadowing effects are included in the geometric optics ray tracing approach.
The size parameter α is defined as α = πD/λ, where D is particle diameter and λ is wavelength.
Materials with electromagnetic signature requirements include architectural coatings, stealth coatings, and metamaterials.
UV radiation transport affects photodegradation; IR radiation transport affects heat transfer in materials.
The computational approach is scalable from nanoscale surface roughness to macroscale surfaces like lunar regolith.
Five separate surface realizations are averaged in simulations to obtain statistically meaningful scattering results.
The suite can predict color change and appearance metamerism in coatings.
Surface scattering models include Kirchhoff, Davies, and Beckmann approaches as classical foundations.
